claim: Sufficient access to transition metals such as iron is essential for bacterial proliferation.
source: Sufficient access to transition metals such as iron is essential for bacterial proliferation and their active limitation within host tissues effectively restricts infection.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Active limitation of transition metals within host tissues effectively restricts infection.
source: Sufficient access to transition metals such as iron is essential for bacterial proliferation and their active limitation within host tissues effectively restricts infection.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus uses the iron-regulated surface determinant (Isd) system to acquire hemoglobin-derived heme.
source: To overcome iron limitation, the invasive pathogen Staphylococcus aureus uses the iron-regulated surface determinant (Isd) system to acquire hemoglobin-derived heme.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Heme transport over the cell wall is well understood.
source: While heme transport over the cell wall is well understood, its transport over the membrane is hardly investigated.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of existing literature in the abstract.

claim: Heme transport over the membrane is hardly investigated.
source: While heme transport over the cell wall is well understood, its transport over the membrane is hardly investigated.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of existing literature in the abstract.

claim: The heme-specific permease IsdF is energized by the general ATPase FhuC.
source: In this study, we show the heme-specific permease IsdF to be energized by the general ATPase FhuC.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including growth assays and BACTH analysis.

claim: IsdF needs appropriate location within the membrane for functionality.
source: Additionally, we show that IsdF needs appropriate location within the membrane for functionality.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The membrane of S. aureus possesses special compartments (functional membrane microdomains [FMMs]) to organize membrane complexes.
source: The membrane of S. aureus possesses special compartments (functional membrane microdomains [FMMs]) to organize membrane complexes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: IsdF is associated with FMMs.
source: We show IsdF to be associated with FMMs, to directly interact with the FMM scaffolding protein flotillin A (FloA) and to co-localize with the latter on intact bacterial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by DRM/DSM fractionation data.

claim: IsdF directly interacts with the FMM scaffolding protein flotillin A (FloA).
source: We show IsdF to be associated with FMMs, to directly interact with the FMM scaffolding protein flotillin A (FloA) and to co-localize with the latter on intact bacterial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: IsdF co-localizes with FloA on intact bacterial cells.
source: We show IsdF to be associated with FMMs, to directly interact with the FMM scaffolding protein flotillin A (FloA) and to co-localize with the latter on intact bacterial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Isd-dependent bacterial growth required FMMs and FloA.
source: Additionally, Isd-dependent bacterial growth required FMMs and FloA.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assays with FMM and FloA mutants.

claim: Isd-dependent heme acquisition requires a highly structured cell envelope to allow coordinated transport over the cell wall and membrane.
source: Our study shows that Isd-dependent heme acquisition requires a highly structured cell envelope to allow coordinated transport over the cell wall and membrane and it gives the first example of a bacterial nutrient acquisition system that depends on FMMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This study gives the first example of a bacterial nutrient acquisition system that depends on FMMs.
source: Our study shows that Isd-dependent heme acquisition requires a highly structured cell envelope to allow coordinated transport over the cell wall and membrane and it gives the first example of a bacterial nutrient acquisition system that depends on FMMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and literature review.

claim: Transition metals such as iron, manganese, copper, and zinc are essential trace elements for all kingdoms of life.
source: Transition metals such as iron, manganese, copper, and zinc are essential trace elements for all kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Transition metals can convert between divalent and trivalent states due to their redox potential.
source: Due to their redox potential, transition metals can convert between divalent and trivalent states making them ideal to support enzymatic processes.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Molecular iron is essential for several central metabolic and cellular processes including glycolysis, oxidative decarboxylation, respiration, and DNA replication.
source: Molecular iron is of major importance in this regard as it is essential for several central metabolic and cellular processes including glycolysis, oxidative decarboxylation, respiration, and DNA replication (Schaible and Kaufmann, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Appropriate acquisition of iron is essential for bacterial growth.
source: Accordingly, appropriate acquisition of iron is essential for bacterial growth and this dependency is a major target for eukaryotic innate immune strategies to limit bacterial infections.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Targeted depletion of human body fluids from trace metals effectively limits bacterial proliferation and is referred to as nutritional immunity.
source: Targeted depletion of human body fluids from trace metals effectively limits bacterial proliferation and is referred to as nutritional immunity (Murdoch and Skaar, 2022; Weinberg, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bacterial pathogens have developed a range of strategies to acquire iron during infection.
source: To overcome host-induced iron starvation, bacterial pathogens have developed a range of strategies to acquire iron during infection (Sheldon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bacterial pathogens can secrete siderophores, which possess sufficient affinity toward Fe3+ to extract the ion from host-chelating molecules.
source: They can secrete siderophores, which possess sufficient affinity toward Fe3+ to extract the ion from host-chelating molecules (e.g. transferrin, lactoferrin) (Miethke and Marahiel, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus secretes the carboxylate-type siderophores staphyloferrin A (SA) and staphyloferrin B (SB).
source: Staphylococcus aureus secretes the carboxylate-type siderophores staphyloferrin A (SA) and staphyloferrin B (SB), and their iron-saturated forms are acquired by the membrane-located HtsABC and SirABC systems, respectively (Beasley et al., 2009; Cheung et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Iron-saturated forms of SA and SB are acquired by the membrane-located HtsABC and SirABC systems, respectively.
source: Staphylococcus aureus secretes the carboxylate-type siderophores staphyloferrin A (SA) and staphyloferrin B (SB), and their iron-saturated forms are acquired by the membrane-located HtsABC and SirABC systems, respectively (Beasley et al., 2009; Cheung et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: S. aureus expresses systems for acquisition of siderophores produced by other bacterial species (xenosiderophores).
source: Additionally, S. aureus expresses systems for acquisition of siderophores produced by other bacterial species (xenosiderophores).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The FhuBGCD1D2 system enables acquisition of hydroxamate-type siderophores.
source: The FhuBGCD1D2 system enables acquisition of hydroxamate-type siderophores (Sebulsky and Heinrichs, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The SstABCD system allows acquisition of iron-chelating molecules of the catecholate-type including xenosiderophores and human-derived catecholamine stress hormones.
source: and the SstABCD system allows acquisition of iron-chelating molecules of the catecholate-type including xenosiderophores, but also human-derived catecholamine stress hormones like epinephrine, norepinephrine, or dopamine (Beasley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The FeoAB transporter presumably allows acquisition of inorganic Fe2+.
source: Moreover, the FeoAB transporter presumably allows acquisition of inorganic Fe2+(Sheldon and Heinrichs, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and uses the qualifier 'presumably' indicating some uncertainty.

claim: In humans, much of the iron is bound to heme in hemoglobin (Hb).
source: In humans, much of the iron is bound to heme in hemoglobin (Hb), which can be released from erythrocytes by the action of cytolytic toxins (Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Spaan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hemoglobin can be released from erythrocytes by the action of cytolytic toxins.
source: In humans, much of the iron is bound to heme in hemoglobin (Hb), which can be released from erythrocytes by the action of cytolytic toxins (Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Spaan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Isd system was first described for the invasive pathogen S. aureus.
source: A well-known mechanism for heme acquisition is the iron-regulated surface determinant (Isd) systems. This was first described for the invasive pathogen S. aureus (Mazmanian et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Similar Isd systems have been identified in Staphylococcus lugdunensis, Staphylococcus capitis, and Staphylococcus caprea.
source: Similar systems have since been identified in Staphylococcus lugdunensis (Heilbronner et al., 2016), Staphylococcus capitis, and Staphylococcus caprea (Sun et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Isd systems have been identified in phylogenetically more distant Gram-positive pathogens such as Bacillus anthracis, Bacillus cereus, and Listeria monocytogenes.
source: as well as in phylogenetically more distant Gram-positive pathogens such as Bacillus anthracis (Gat et al., 2008; Maresso et al., 2006), Bacillus cereus (Abi-Khalil et al., 2015), and Listeria monocytogenes (Klebba et al., 2012; Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All Isd systems contain surface-anchored molecules to extract heme from host hemoproteins and to guide it over the cell wall to a membrane-located ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter.
source: All Isd systems contain surface-anchored molecules to extract heme from host hemoproteins and to guide it over the cell wall to a membrane-located ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter.
evidence: This is stated as a general characteristic of Isd systems based on existing knowledge.

claim: In the cytosol, the heme is degraded to release ionic iron.
source: In the cytosol, the heme is degraded to release ionic iron.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Isd systems.

claim: The Isd system of S. aureus is best studied.
source: The Isd system of S. aureus is best studied (Sheldon and Heinrichs, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: The cell wall-anchored proteins IsdB and IsdH bind Hb and Hb-haptoglobin complexes, respectively.
source: Here, the cell wall-anchored proteins (CWAs) IsdB and IsdH bind Hb and Hb-haptoglobin complexes, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the S. aureus Isd system.

claim: Heme is removed from the hemoproteins by IsdA and IsdB and transferred to IsdC in the cell wall.
source: Heme is removed from the hemoproteins by IsdA and IsdB and transferred to IsdC in the cell wall.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the S. aureus Isd system.

claim: Heme is transferred from IsdC to the heme-specific lipoprotein IsdE on the outer leaflet of the cell membrane.
source: Heme is then transferred to the heme-specific lipoprotein IsdE on the outer leaflet of the cell membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the S. aureus Isd system.

claim: The permease IsdF functions as homodimer and transports heme into the cytosol.
source: The permease IsdF functions as homodimer and transports heme into the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the S. aureus Isd system.

claim: The two monooxygenases IsdG and IsdI release iron from heme in the cytosol.
source: There, the two monooxygenases IsdG and IsdI release iron from heme.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the S. aureus Isd system.

claim: The passage of heme across the cell wall of S. aureus has been studied in great detail.
source: The passage of heme across the cell wall of S. aureus has been studied in great detail.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of existing literature.

claim: The process of heme transport across the membrane remains somewhat undefined.
source: In contrast, the process of heme transport across the membrane remains somewhat undefined.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of existing literature and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: An ATPase is not encoded within the isd operon of S. aureus.
source: Importantly, an ATPase is not encoded within the isd operon of S. aureus, raising the question of how the transport of heme is energized.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from genomic data.

claim: Bacterial membranes represent highly structured cellular compartments.
source: It is increasingly recognized that bacterial membranes represent highly structured cellular compartments.
evidence: This is stated as emerging knowledge in the field.

claim: Functional membrane microdomains (FMMs) have gained increasing attention in recent years.
source: In this regard, functional membrane microdomains (FMMs) have gained increasing attention in the recent years (Bach and Bramkamp, 2013; Bramkamp and Lopez, 2015; Farnoud et al., 2015; López and Kolter, 2010; Matsumoto et al., 2006; Yokoyama and Matsui, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: FMMs in S. aureus consist of the polyisoprenoid staphyloxanthin and its derivative lipids.
source: FMMs are specific domains in the bacterial membrane that, in the case of S. aureus, consist of the polyisoprenoid staphyloxanthin and its derivative lipids.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FMMs in S. aureus.

claim: An intrinsic characteristic of FMMs is the structural protein flotillin A (FloA) recruiting proteins to the FMMs and promoting their oligomerization.
source: An intrinsic characteristic of FMMs is the structural protein flotillin A (FloA) recruiting proteins to the FMMs and promoting their oligomerization (Bramkamp and Lopez, 2015; López and Kolter, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: FMMs have been shown to be crucial to coordinate diverse cellular functions in S. aureus.
source: FMMs have been shown to be crucial to coordinate diverse cellular functions in S. aureus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: FMMs control activity of cell wall biosynthetic enzymes such as PBP2a and are essential for expression of resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA).
source: On one hand, they control activity of cell wall biosynthetic enzymes such as PBP2a and are essential for expression of resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) (García-Fernández et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Several membrane-associated processes such as the secretion of type VII secretion effector proteins depend on FloA.
source: On the other hand, several membrane-associated processes such as the secretion of type VII secretion effector proteins (Mielich-Süss et al., 2017) or the RNase Rny depend on FloA (Koch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The RNase Rny depends on FloA.
source: On the other hand, several membrane-associated processes such as the secretion of type VII secretion effector proteins (Mielich-Süss et al., 2017) or the RNase Rny depend on FloA (Koch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bacterial two-hybrid assays show direct interaction between the iron-responsive ATPase FhuC and the heme permease protein IsdF.
source: In this study, we have used bacterial two-hybrid assays to show direct interaction between the iron-responsive ATPase FhuC and the heme permease protein IsdF.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by BACTH data.

claim: Hb-dependent growth requires FhuC activity.
source: Additionally, we have shown that Hb-dependent growth requires FhuC activity, suggesting that FhuC energizes heme transport in S. aureus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assay data.

claim: FhuC energizes heme transport in S. aureus.
source: Additionally, we have shown that Hb-dependent growth requires FhuC activity, suggesting that FhuC energizes heme transport in S. aureus.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth assay data showing FhuC requirement for Hb-dependent growth.

claim: The heme permease IsdF was shown to be associated with FMMs.
source: Moreover, the heme permease IsdF was shown to be associated with FMMs, to interact directly with FloA and to co-localize with the latter in the bacterial envelope.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by DRM/DSM fractionation data.

claim: IsdF interacts directly with FloA.
source: Moreover, the heme permease IsdF was shown to be associated with FMMs, to interact directly with FloA and to co-localize with the latter in the bacterial envelope.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: IsdF co-localizes with FloA in the bacterial envelope.
source: Moreover, the heme permease IsdF was shown to be associated with FMMs, to interact directly with FloA and to co-localize with the latter in the bacterial envelope.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Hb-dependent proliferation was reliant on the correct formation of FMMs.
source: Accordingly, Hb-dependent proliferation was reliant on the correct formation of FMMs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assays with FMM mutants.

claim: Appropriate FMM formation is required for Isd-dependent proliferation of S. lugdunensis.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that appropriate FMM formation is also required for Isd-dependent proliferation of S. lugdunensis, suggesting that FMM-dependent structuring of the membrane is crucial for the functionality of Isd systems in staphylococci.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assays with S. lugdunensis mutants.

claim: FMM-dependent structuring of the membrane is crucial for the functionality of Isd systems in staphylococci.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that appropriate FMM formation is also required for Isd-dependent proliferation of S. lugdunensis, suggesting that FMM-dependent structuring of the membrane is crucial for the functionality of Isd systems in staphylococci.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing FMM requirement in both S. aureus and S. lugdunensis.

claim: A S. aureus USA300 JE2 fhuC::Erm mutant showed significantly reduced growth when human Hb was supplied as a sole source of nutrient iron.
source: We found that a S. aureus USA300 JE2 fhuC::Erm mutant, obtained from the Nebraska transposon mutant library (Fey et al., 2013), showed significantly reduced growth when human Hb (hHb) was supplied as a sole source of nutrient iron (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The growth deficit of the fhuC mutant was rescued by addition of iron(II) sulfate.
source: This deficit was rescued by addition of iron(II) sulfate (Figure 1B), suggesting that FhuC energizes heme transport across the membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fhuC-deficient strain showed a pronounced growth deficit in the presence of Hb.
source: Again, the fhuC-deficient strain showed a pronounced growth deficit in the presence of Hb.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by growth assay data.

claim: Plasmid-based expression of FhuC restored Hb-dependent growth.
source: Importantly, plasmid-based expression of FhuC restored Hb-dependent growth (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FhuC is needed for Isd-dependent heme acquisition.
source: This supports the idea that FhuC is needed for Isd-dependent heme acquisition.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth and complementation data.

claim: Co-expression of FhuC with its native permease FhuB generated distinct positive signals in BACTH.
source: Co-expression of FhuC with its native permease FhuB as well as with IsdF generated distinct positive signals (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by BACTH data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Co-expression of FhuC with IsdF generated distinct positive signals in BACTH.
source: Co-expression of FhuC with its native permease FhuB as well as with IsdF generated distinct positive signals (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by BACTH data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Co-expression of FhuC with the iron-independent permease MntB did not result in detectable LacZ activity.
source: In contrast, co-expression of FhuC with the iron-independent permease MntB (manganese uptake) did not result in detectable LacZ activity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by BACTH data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FhuC energizes the heme transport system IsdEF.
source: This suggests that FhuC energizes the heme transport system IsdEF and structural characteristics within the permease must allow discrimination of FhuC targets and non-targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the BACTH data showing interaction between FhuC and IsdF but not MntB.

claim: Structural characteristics within the permease must allow discrimination of FhuC targets and non-targets.
source: This suggests that FhuC energizes the heme transport system IsdEF and structural characteristics within the permease must allow discrimination of FhuC targets and non-targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the BACTH data showing selective interaction of FhuC.

claim: Within all putative coupling helixes only a single glycine residue (G217 in IsdF) is conserved.
source: This analysis showed that within all putative coupling helixes only a single glycine residue (G217 in IsdF) is conserved.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: A single alanine residue (A213 in IsdF) was conserved in all iron compound permeases but not in MntB.
source: Additionally, a single alanine residue (A213 in IsdF) was conserved in all iron compound permeases but not in MntB (Figure 2B+C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis shown in figures.

claim: Exchange of alanine 213 to phenylalanine (A213F) did not prevent interaction with FhuC.
source: Exchange of the alanine 213 to the bulky amino acid phenylalanine (A213F) did not prevent interaction with FhuC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from BACTH analysis with mutant proteins.

claim: Exchange of glycine 217 to phenylalanine (G217F) did not prevent interaction with FhuC.
source: The same was true when glycine 217 was exchanged for phenylalanine (G217F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from BACTH analysis with mutant proteins.

claim: Combination of both substitutions (A213F and G217F) abrogated the interaction between IsdF and FhuC.
source: However, combination of both substitutions abrogated the interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from BACTH analysis with double mutant protein shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A213 and G217 are important for the recognition of FhuC.
source: These results show the importance of A213 and G217 for the recognition of FhuC, but they do not explain how MntB and IsdF are discriminated.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The coupling helix of IsdF inserted into MntB did not allow interaction with FhuC.
source: Interestingly, the resulting fusion protein remained negative in BACTH analysis with FhuC (Figure 2D), suggesting that the sequence and structure of the coupling helix alone is not sufficient to allow FhuC to discriminate between IsdF and MntB.
evidence: This is a primary finding from BACTH analysis with fusion protein shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The sequence and structure of the coupling helix alone is not sufficient to allow FhuC to discriminate between IsdF and MntB.
source: Interestingly, the resulting fusion protein remained negative in BACTH analysis with FhuC (Figure 2D), suggesting that the sequence and structure of the coupling helix alone is not sufficient to allow FhuC to discriminate between IsdF and MntB.
evidence: This is inferred from the fusion protein BACTH data.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain (short_1) did not affect the interaction with FhuC.
source: Deletion of the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain (short_1) did not affect the interaction with FhuC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from BACTH analysis with truncated proteins.

claim: Truncation at the fourth cytosolic loop (short_2) abrogated the interaction with FhuC.
source: However, truncation at the fourth cytosolic loop (short_2) abrogated the interaction and the same was true for additional truncations lacking more extended C-terminal fragments (short_3/short_4) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from BACTH analysis with truncated proteins shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Besides the coupling helix, the C-terminal part of IsdF is crucial for appropriate formation of the IsdF-FhuC complex.
source: These data indicate that besides the coupling helix, the C-terminal part of IsdF is crucial for appropriate formation of the IsdF-FhuC complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the truncation BACTH data.

claim: A high number of iron uptake-associated proteins are enriched in the FMM-containing membrane fraction including the heme transport system IsdEF and the siderophore transporters Fhu, Hts, and Sir.
source: Revisiting these datasets showed that a high number of iron uptake-associated proteins are enriched in the FMM-containing membrane fraction including the heme transport system IsdEF and the siderophore transporters Fhu, Hts, and Sir.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of previously published proteomic data.

claim: 80% of the IsdF signal was detected in the DRM fraction.
source: In contrast, quantitative western blotting showed that 80% of the IsdF signal was detected in the DRM fraction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from DRM/DSM fractionation shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IsdF is predominantly associated with the DRM fraction.
source: This confirms that IsdF is predominantly associated with the DRM fraction and suggests that IsdF is localized within FMMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the DRM/DSM fractionation data.

claim: IsdF is localized within FMMs.
source: This confirms that IsdF is predominantly associated with the DRM fraction and suggests that IsdF is localized within FMMs.
evidence: This is inferred from the DRM/DSM fractionation data.

claim: IsdF was three times more abundant in the Ni-NTA eluate of the FloA-His expressing strain compared to FloA WT.
source: However, IsdF was three times more abundant in the Ni-NTA eluate of the FloA-His expressing strain (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IsdF interacts with FloA which allows co-purification.
source: This strongly suggests that IsdF interacts with FloA which allows co-purification.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: FloA signals formed distinct foci at the bacterial surface most likely representing FMMs.
source: As described previously, FloA signals formed distinct foci at the bacterial surface most likely representing FMMs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A, consistent with previous reports.

claim: IsdF accumulated in patches.
source: Interestingly, IsdF also accumulated in patches (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IsdF and FloA signals showed a perfect overlap in 7.5% of measurements.
source: This showed a perfect overlap in 7.5% of measurements while maxima were separated by a single pixel (0.0645 µM) or by two pixels (0.129 µM) in 29.5% and 26.7% of cases, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: IsdF and FloA maxima were separated by a single pixel in 29.5% of cases.
source: This showed a perfect overlap in 7.5% of measurements while maxima were separated by a single pixel (0.0645 µM) or by two pixels (0.129 µM) in 29.5% and 26.7% of cases, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: IsdF and FloA maxima were separated by two pixels in 26.7% of cases.
source: This showed a perfect overlap in 7.5% of measurements while maxima were separated by a single pixel (0.0645 µM) or by two pixels (0.129 µM) in 29.5% and 26.7% of cases, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Fluorescent signals derived from plasmid pCQ11:isdF-mNeongreen were strong in a FloA expressing strain but almost undetectable in a floA-deficient mutant.
source: Furthermore, we found that fluorescent signals derived from plasmid pCQ11:isdF-mNeongreen were strong in a FloA expressing strain but almost undetectable in a floA-deficient mutant (Figure 4C+D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Replacement of the mutant floA allele with the functional WT allele restored IsdF signals to WT level.
source: Replacement of the mutant allele with the functional WT allele (Newman floA_R) by allelic exchange restored IsdF signals to WT level (Figure 4C+D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: FloA is crucial for the appropriate incorporation and spatial distribution of IsdF within the membrane of S. aureus.
source: These data suggest that FloA is crucial for the appropriate incorporation and spatial distribution of IsdF within the membrane of S. aureus.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence microscopy data showing FloA-dependent IsdF localization.

claim: A USA300 JE2 floA:Erm mutant showed significant growth reduction when Hb was supplied as the sole source of nutrient iron.
source: Growth in the presence of FeSO4 was not impacted by this mutation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), but a significant growth reduction was observed when Hb was supplied as the sole source of nutrient iron.
evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays.

claim: Replacement of the mutant floA allele with the functional WT allele restored full growth on Hb.
source: Replacement of the mutant allele with the functional WT allele (JE2 floA_R) by allelic exchange restored full growth (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FloA-dependent incorporation of IsdF is needed for heme acquisition.
source: These data support the idea that FloA-dependent incorporation of IsdF is needed for heme acquisition.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth and complementation data.

claim: S. aureus Newman Δisd, ΔfloA, and ΔcrtM mutants showed WT levels of growth in the presence of FeSO4.
source: All mutants showed WT levels of growth in the presence of FeSO4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) but had a comparable growth deficit in the presence of Hb (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S. aureus Newman Δisd, ΔfloA, and ΔcrtM mutants had a comparable growth deficit in the presence of Hb.
source: All mutants showed WT levels of growth in the presence of FeSO4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) but had a comparable growth deficit in the presence of Hb (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Blockage of FMM biosynthesis by zaragozic acid reduced Hb-dependent growth.
source: Additionally, blockage of FMM biosynthesis by zaragozic acid (ZA) (López and Kolter, 2010) reduced Hb-dependent growth (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays with ZA shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The reduced growth of the fhuC mutant was not further decreased by the addition of ZA.

evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Growth of the ΔlhaSTA mutant reflects Isd-dependent proliferation in S. lugdunensis.

claim: Functional FMMs are important for Isd-dependent heme acquisition in S. lugdunensis.

claim: Inactivation of floA in S. lugdunensis WT did not influence Hb-dependent growth.

claim: Activity of LhaSTA does not depend on FMMs.

claim: LhaSTA allows inhibition of the Isd system to be by-passed.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of floA in S. lugdunensis WT did not influence Hb-dependent growth, suggesting that activity of LhaSTA does not depend on FMMs and allows inhibition of the Isd system to be by-passed.

claim: ABC transporters are classical molecular machines that transport nutrients across biological membranes and allow their accumulation against concentration gradients at the cost of ATP.
source: ABC transporters are classical molecular machines that transport nutrients across biological membranes and allow their accumulation against concentration gradients at the cost of ATP (Rees et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Prokaryotic ABC-type importers consist of three functionally distinct subunits: an extracellular substrate-binding protein, a membrane-located permease and a cytosolic ATPase.
source: Prokaryotic ABC-type importers consist of three functionally distinct subunits, an extracellular substrate-binding protein (SBP), a membrane-located permease and a cytosolic ATPase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, SBPs are located in the periplasmic space.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, SBPs are located in the periplasmic space while the SBPs of Gram-positive bacteria are lipoproteins that are coupled to the extracellular leaflet of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The SBPs of Gram-positive bacteria are lipoproteins that are coupled to the extracellular leaflet of the membrane.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, SBPs are located in the periplasmic space while the SBPs of Gram-positive bacteria are lipoproteins that are coupled to the extracellular leaflet of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A single ATPase can energize several permeases with different substrates.
source: It is known that a single ATPase can energize several permeases with different substrates (Quentin et al., 1999) including the iron compound permeases of S. aureus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FhuC is needed for staphyloferrin-dependent proliferation.
source: It has been shown that FhuC, the ATPase encoded within the hydroxamate siderophore transport system fhuCBG, is needed for staphyloferrin-dependent proliferation (Beasley et al., 2009; Sebulsky et al., 2000; Speziali et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deletion of fhuC has a major impact on Hb-dependent growth.
source: Here, we show that deletion of fhuC has a major impact on Hb-dependent growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by growth assay data.

claim: FhuC is a housekeeping ATPase that powers acquisition of different iron compounds by S. aureus.
source: This suggests that FhuC is a housekeeping ATPase that powers acquisition of different iron compounds by S. aureus.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing FhuC requirement for multiple iron acquisition systems.

claim: Weak Hb-dependent growth was observed with the ΔfhuC mutant.
source: However, weak Hb-dependent growth was observed with the ΔfhuC mutant.
evidence: This is a primary finding from growth assays.

claim: An unknown ATPase might partially substitute for the function of FhuC.
source: This could indicate that an unknown ATPase partially substitutes for the function of FhuC.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of residual growth in the fhuC mutant.

claim: Seven ABC iron compound transporters were previously identified in the genome of S. aureus.
source: Seven ABC iron compound transporters were previously identified in the genome of S. aureus (Sst, Fhu, Sir, Hts, Isd systems, SAUSA300_1514–1517 and SAUSA300_0598–99) with SstC and SAUSA300_1516 being ATPases besides FhuC (Skaar et al., 2004).

claim: SstC and SAUSA300_1516 are ATPases besides FhuC in S. aureus.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It seems possible that SstC and SAUSA300_1516 are able to partly substitute for FhuC.
source: It seems possible that these are able to partly substitute for FhuC.
evidence: This is speculation based on the existence of other ATPases and residual growth in fhuC mutant.

claim: A secondary heme transporter might exist in S. aureus.
source: Alternatively, a secondary heme transporter might exist in S. aureus.
evidence: This is speculation to explain residual growth in fhuC mutant.

source: It is worth considering that Isd-dependent heme acquisition in other pathogens appears to be energized by specialized ATPases.

claim: Similar cases of ATPases energizing a variety of importers have been reported for other species.
source: Similar cases of ATPases energizing a variety of importers have been reported for other species such as Streptococcus pneumoniae (Linke et al., 2013; Marion et al., 2011), Streptococcus suis (Tan et al., 2015), Streptomyces reticuli (Schlösser, 2000), Streptomyces lividans (Hurtubise et al., 1995), and Bacillus subtilis (Ferreira et al., 2017; Ferreira and Sá-Nogueira, 2010; Morabbi Heravi et al., 2019; Schönert et al., 2006).

claim: Type I importers typically have permeases with only six transmembrane domains and acquire substrates like ions, amino acids, and sugars.
source: Type I importers typically have permeases with only six transmembrane domains (TMDs) and acquire substrates like ions, amino acids, and sugars.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ABC transporter classification.

source: In contrast, type II importer permeases consist of 10 TMDs and take up bigger substrates like heme or cobalamin (Locher, 2009).

claim: Coupling helices often contain an EAA motif to facilitate interaction with an ATPase.

claim: The secondary structures of coupling helices are important for the recruitment of ATPases.

source: However, we found that disruption of FMMs by mutation of floA interfered with Isd-dependent proliferation but not siderophore-dependent growth.

claim: The heme funnel is thought to allow concerted passage of heme over the envelope.
